We additionally report \textbf{Leave-One-Family-Out (LOFO)} results, where an entire model family (e.g., all Qwen models) is held out, testing generalization across architectural lineages.

\paragraph{Classifier.}
We use XGBoost \cite{xgboost} as the classifier throughout.
Gradient-boosted trees handle heterogeneous feature scales and nonlinear interactions without extensive hyperparameter tuning, and their feature importance scores support interpretability.
We use $n\_\text{estimators}{=}200$, $\max\_\text{depth}{=}6$, and learning rate $0.1$ for the 7-feature ensemble.
Baseline detectors (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines}) use the same XGBoost framework with $n\_\text{estimators}{=}100$ and $\max\_\text{depth}{=}3$ to avoid overfitting their single-feature input.
LOGO F1 is stable across random seeds (mean\,=\,0.789, std\,=\,0.0009 over 5 seeds), confirming that results are not sensitive to classifier initialization.
Alternative classifiers (random forest, logistic regression) yield comparable performance (Appendix~\ref{app:classifier}), confirming that discriminative power resides in the features, not the classifier.
We evaluated two ordinal-specific methods (CORAL \cite{coral_ordinal}, Frank-Hall ordinal ensemble \cite{frank_hall_ordinal}); neither significantly outperforms multiclass XGBoost (3-class LOGO F1 0.771--0.793 vs.\ 0.789, CIs overlapping), confirming that with only three ordinal levels, ordinal structure provides minimal additional benefit.

\paragraph{Metrics and statistical testing.}
The primary metric is \textbf{macro-averaged F1} over the three depth classes, which weights minority classes (gen-1, gen-2+) equally against the typically easier gen-0 class.
We report per-class F1 scores and 95\% confidence intervals via \emph{percentile bootstrap} ($n{=}1{,}000$), resampling at the document level within each held-out fold.
For pairwise model comparisons (e.g., full features vs.\ ablated subsets), we use the \textbf{McNemar test} on disagreement tables.
For comparisons against detection baselines, we use \textbf{paired bootstrap} significance tests.
All reported $p$-values are two-sided.
We report six pairwise comparisons in \S\ref{sec:results-baselines}; applying Bonferroni correction ($\alpha_{\text{adj}} = 0.05/6 = 0.0083$), all remain significant at $p < 0.001$.
Feature--depth correlations (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) are computed on class-balanced subsamples (equal samples per depth class) to control for depth-class imbalance in the generation pipeline.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Shape stationarity: mechanistic hypothesis.}
Distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay) remain near-stationary across generation depths, while central-tendency features drift monotonically (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
We hypothesize that this reflects a decomposition of the autoregressive generation process: at each token position, the output distribution is determined jointly by model parameters (fixed) and conditioning context (varying).
Recursive generation progressively shifts context toward the model's high-probability regions---reducing entropy mean---but does not alter the softmax architecture or sampling hyperparameters that determine distributional shape.
This predicts that shape features should remain stationary until generation depth reaches the model's fixed-point distribution, a regime not yet observed in our chain lengths ($\leq$4 steps).
Sampling ablation is consistent with this account: depth signal is robust to moderate temperature variation (${\leq}0.3$\,pp for $t \in [0.5, 0.7]$) but degrades substantially at $t = 1.0$ ($-6$\,pp; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}), where the sampling mechanism itself becomes the dominant source of distributional shape variation, overwhelming the depth signal.

\paragraph{Prompt-type dependence.}
Differential depth response strength varies substantially across prompt types.
Continuation chains exhibit 16.9\% depth retention loss by gen-4, while elaboration chains retain 98.6\% of samples (Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}).
The 7-feature ensemble achieves within-type CV F1 of 0.781 for continuation vs.\ 0.730 for elaboration; cross-prompt-type transfer (LOPTO F1\,=\,0.753) confirms shared signal despite differing drift magnitudes.
These results bound depth fingerprinting's applicability: in near-paraphrastic settings (elaboration, rewriting), distributional drift attenuates more rapidly, consistent with semantic-preservation constraints acting as an anchor against distributional shift \cite{broken_telephone}.

\paragraph{Corpus-level vs.\ document-level utility.}
The practical value of depth estimation depends on the unit of analysis.
At the individual document level, gen-1 per-class F1\,=\,0.64 implies a 36\% misclassification rate---insufficient for automated filtering but suitable for flagging suspect documents for human review.
At the corpus level, aggregate depth composition can be estimated with substantially lower error: over $n$ documents, estimation error scales as $O(1/\sqrt{n})$, making corpus-level provenance characterization reliable even with moderate per-document accuracy.
The 3-class design explicitly targets the most informative boundaries: human vs.\ machine (gen-0 vs.\ gen-1+) and shallow vs.\ deep recursion (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+), where the distributional distinction is most actionable.

\paragraph{Relation to model collapse.}
Our results relate to, but are distinct from, model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse,self_consuming_mad}.
Model collapse describes distributional degradation when models are \emph{retrained} on their own outputs; we observe analogous drift---monotonic decrease in vocabulary diversity, compression of perplexity---in \emph{inference chains} without parameter updates.
Quantitatively, the magnitude differs: hapax ratio declines ${\sim}$14\% across 4 inference-chain depths, compared to catastrophic diversity loss reported after 5--10 retraining generations \cite{curse_of_recursion}.
We hypothesize that inference-chain drift represents an early, reversible stage of the same distributional narrowing process that becomes irreversible only when gradient updates amplify the shift.
This suggests depth fingerprinting features could serve as leading indicators: text exhibiting inference-chain drift signatures would, if recycled into training, accelerate the collapse regime.
Topic drift mediates rather than confounds this process: semantic narrowing accounts for less than 9\% of feature variance (maximum $R^2 = 0.082$ for entropy\_mean), and shape features are near-independent of semantic drift ($|\rho| = 0.068$).

\paragraph{Granularity ceiling.}
Five-class depth estimation reduces LOGO F1 from 0.789 to 0.501; gen-2 and gen-3 are inseparable (per-class F1\,$\approx$\,0.26), establishing three classes as the practical ceiling for handcrafted features (Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}).
QLoRA fine-tuning raises 3-class F1 to 0.905 (+11.6\,pp; Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}), confirming exploitable depth signal beyond summary statistics.

\paragraph{Robustness to post-generation editing.}
Depth features degrade gracefully under simulated editing: 20\% random token replacement reduces 3-class F1 by only 6.0\,pp, while LLM rephrasing drops binary F1 by 6.3\,pp (Appendix~\ref{app:human-edit}).
This asymmetry---surface noise is tolerable, systematic distributional manipulation is not---is consistent with depth signal residing in aggregate distributional properties rather than individual token choices.

\paragraph{Paraphrastic chains.}
Initial paraphrastic experiments exhibited reversed entropy--depth correlations ($\rho = +0.394$), but removing contaminated samples aligned correlations with continuation chains ($\rho = -0.533$), confirming the reversal was an artifact.
On clean data, paraphrastic chains achieve binary F1\,=\,0.671 (vs.\ 0.749 for continuation), consistent with faster convergence under semantic-preservation constraints \cite{broken_telephone}.
Cross-transfer is effective (para$\to$cont F1\,=\,0.770, cont$\to$para 0.743), indicating shared depth signal.

\paragraph{Instruct tuning.}
Instruction-tuned models show substantially weaker depth fingerprints (OLMo-Instruct LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 vs.\ 0.764 base; Qwen3-0.6B-Instruct 0.667 vs.\ 0.816 base under the 7-generator split; base-only yields 0.824, Table~\ref{tab:logo-results}).
Length-matched controls reduce correlations to near zero (all $|\rho| < 0.02$ for Qwen3-0.6B), and binary classification is near chance (F1\,$\approx$\,0.5), indicating that depth signal is not operationally detectable in instruct chains.
This justifies our restriction to base models: instruction tuning introduces distributional effects (output length regulation, format constraints) that dominate the subtler recursive drift signal, making base models the appropriate setting for isolating the generation mechanism.

\paragraph{Negative downstream finding.}
Depth-aware curation does not improve downstream language model quality over random subsampling (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).
This negative result carries positive information value: it rules out depth-based filtering as a data selection strategy, sparing practitioners from building depth-conditional pipelines that would not yield quality gains.
The dominant factor is data quantity, not depth composition---consistent with findings emphasizing data volume over curation sophistication \cite{self_consuming_mad}.

1	\section{Method}
2	\label{sec:method}
3	
4	\subsection{Task Formulation}
5	\label{sec:task}
6	
7	Given a text $x$, the goal is to predict its \emph{generation depth} $d \in \{0, 1, 2{+}\}$, where $d{=}0$ denotes human-written text, $d{=}1$ denotes first-generation LLM output conditioned on human text, and $d{=}2{+}$ denotes text produced by recursively conditioning an LLM on its own prior output at least twice.
8	Formally, let $\mathcal{C}_0$ be a reference corpus of human-written text.
9	A generation chain of depth $k$ is defined recursively: $x^{(0)} \sim \mathcal{C}_0$, and $x^{(k)} = G(x^{(k-1)})$ for $k \geq 1$, where $G$ denotes stochastic LLM generation conditioned on its input.
10	We frame depth estimation as an ordinal classification task over three classes rather than binary real-vs-synthetic detection, enabling finer-grained provenance characterization.
11	Depths beyond 2 are merged into a single $2{+}$ class, consistent with monotonic feature convergence that compresses inter-class margins beyond depth 2 (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
12	
13	\subsection{Generation Chain Construction}
14	\label{sec:generation}
15	
16	We construct generation chains using eight generators spanning five model families: \textbf{Pythia} (2.8B, 1B) \cite{pythia}, \textbf{OLMo} (OLMo-2-1B) \cite{olmo}, \textbf{Qwen} (Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-8B-Base) \cite{qwen3}, \textbf{Llama} (Llama-3.2-3B) \cite{llama3}, and \textbf{Mistral} (Mistral-7B-v0.3) \cite{mistral7b}.
17	This selection covers parameter scales from 0.6B to 8B and diverse pretraining corpora, enabling evaluation of cross-generator and cross-scale generalization.
18	
19	For each generator, we sample approximately 1{,}000 seed passages from English Wikipedia as $\mathcal{C}_0$.
20	The same pool of seed passages serves as gen-0 for all generators.
21	We use shared seeds across generators to ensure that cross-generator comparisons control for input content, isolating the effect of the generation model from source text variation.
22	In LOGO evaluation, gen-0 samples from the held-out generator's chains also appear (with the same text) in the training generators' chains, creating a potential train--test overlap for the gen-0 class.
23	We address this with a supplementary binary evaluation excluding gen-0 entirely (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines}).
24	Each seed is iteratively fed through the generator to produce a chain of depth 4 (i.e., gen-0 through gen-4), using the prompt ``\texttt{Continue the following text: \{text\}}''.
25	All generation uses temperature $\tau{=}0.7$, nucleus sampling with $p{=}0.9$, and maximum length of 256 new tokens.
26	The theoretical yield is $8 \times {\sim}1{,}000 \times 5 \approx 40{,}000$ texts; after removing generation failures, exact duplicates, and passages shorter than 50 tokens, 37{,}058 texts remain.
27	For classification, depths 2--4 are collapsed into the $2{+}$ class.
28	
29	\subsection{Feature Extraction}
30	\label{sec:features}
31	
32	The seven features are motivated by two complementary views of distributional drift.
33	Reference-model features capture how the text's token-level surprise distribution shifts relative to a fixed model; surface features capture how lexical diversity contracts under recursive generation.
34	Together, they span both the generative mechanism (what the model produces) and the surface manifestation (how the vocabulary changes).
35	This two-pronged design is not post-hoc: it follows directly from the hypothesis that recursive generation induces a location shift in the NLL distribution (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
36	
37	We extract seven distributional features per text, organized into two groups based on what they measure rather than how they are computed.
38	
39	\paragraph{Reference-model features.}
40	A held-out reference model (Pythia-410M, chosen to be smaller than all generators) computes per-token negative log-likelihood (NLL) for each text.
41	Although Pythia-410M shares the GPT-NeoX architecture with two of the eight generators, cross-family reference model experiments (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) confirm that depth features are not reference-specific (LOGO F1 varies by only 0.024 across Pythia, OLMo, and Qwen references).
42	From the resulting NLL sequence, we extract five statistics:
43	\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
44	    \item \textbf{entropy\_mean}\footnote{We use ``entropy'' as shorthand for token-level negative log-likelihood under the reference model, following convention in prior detection work. These are point-wise NLL values, not Shannon entropy of the full distribution.}: mean token-level NLL, capturing the average predictability of the text under the reference model;
45	    \item \textbf{entropy\_std}: standard deviation of token-level NLL, measuring the spread of per-token surprise;
46	    \item \textbf{entropy\_max}: maximum token-level NLL, capturing the most surprising token;
47	    \item \textbf{entropy\_min}: minimum token-level NLL, capturing the most predictable token---as generation depth increases, the floor of token-level surprise drops, reflecting the model's increasing confidence on its own outputs.
48	    Although entropy\_min shows near-zero marginal impact in leave-one-feature-out analysis ($\Delta$F1\,=\,+0.01\,pp), we retain it for completeness of the NLL summary statistics (mean, std, max, min) and because removing it does not improve performance;
49	    \item \textbf{tail\_decay}: proportion of tokens whose NLL exceeds the 90th percentile of the reference distribution (computed over $\mathcal{C}_0$), measuring how heavy-tailed the NLL distribution is relative to human text.
50	    Sensitivity analysis confirms stable classification (F1 variation ${<}$0.3\,pp) across thresholds from the 85th to 95th percentile.
51	\end{itemize}
52	
53	\paragraph{Surface features.}
54	Two features capture lexical diversity without requiring a reference model:
55	\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
56	    \item \textbf{TTR}: type-token ratio (number of unique word types divided by total tokens);
57	    \item \textbf{hapax\_ratio}: proportion of words appearing exactly once (\emph{hapax legomena}).
58	\end{itemize}
59	
60	\paragraph{Feature complementarity.}
61	The grouping reflects an empirical pattern we term \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity features (entropy\_mean, TTR, hapax\_ratio) show strong monotonic drift with generation depth ($|\rho| = 0.61$--$0.65$); entropy\_min and entropy\_std show moderate drift ($|\rho| = 0.20$--$0.41$); and upper-tail features (entropy\_max, tail\_decay) remain near-stationary ($|\rho| < 0.05$).
62	This differential behavior---consistent with recursive generation compressing the lower tail of the NLL distribution while preserving upper-tail behavior---motivates combining both feature types.
63	As shown in \S\ref{sec:results}, the full 7-feature set significantly outperforms either group alone.

66	\label{sec:evaluation}
67	
68	\paragraph{Cross-validation.}
69	To evaluate generalization to unseen generators, we use \textbf{Leave-One-Generator-Out (LOGO)} cross-validation: in each fold, one of the eight generators is held out for testing and the remaining seven provide training data.
70	We additionally report \textbf{Leave-One-Family-Out (LOFO)} results, where an entire model family (e.g., all Qwen models) is held out, testing generalization across architectural lineages.
71	
72	\paragraph{Classifier.}
73	We use XGBoost \cite{xgboost} as the classifier throughout.
74	Gradient-boosted trees handle heterogeneous feature scales and nonlinear interactions without extensive hyperparameter tuning, and their feature importance scores support interpretability.
75	We use $n\_\text{estimators}{=}200$, $\max\_\text{depth}{=}6$, and learning rate $0.1$ for the 7-feature ensemble.
76	Baseline detectors (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines}) use the same XGBoost framework with $n\_\text{estimators}{=}100$ and $\max\_\text{depth}{=}3$ to avoid overfitting their single-feature input.

To assess whether depth features are robust to post-generation human editing, we simulate two editing scenarios on the full generation chain dataset and re-evaluate the 6-generator LOGO pipeline (Table~\ref{tab:human-edit}).

\paragraph{Random token replacement.}
We randomly replace 5\%, 10\%, or 20\% of tokens in each text with uniformly sampled vocabulary items, simulating unstructured human edits (typo corrections, word substitutions).
Classification degrades gracefully: 3-class F1 drops by 3.5\,pp at 5\% replacement and 6.0\,pp at 20\%, while binary F1 (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) remains nearly unchanged ($\Delta \leq 0.8$\,pp).
The asymmetry is expected---random edits primarily disrupt human-vs-machine separation (gen-0 classification) by injecting noise into surface features, but the depth-discriminative distributional signal between gen-1 and gen-2+ is distributed across enough tokens to survive moderate perturbation.

\paragraph{LLM rephrase.}
We rephrase each text using an instruction-tuned LLM, simulating the common scenario where users lightly edit LLM-generated text with LLM assistance.
Three-class F1 drops modestly ($-3.4$\,pp), comparable to 5\% random replacement.
However, binary F1 drops substantially ($-6.3$\,pp), indicating that LLM rephrasing specifically erodes the distributional differences between generation depths---consistent with the rephraser imposing its own distributional signature that partially overwrites the depth fingerprint.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{Human-edit robustness under 6-gen LOGO evaluation. Baseline uses unmodified generation chains.}
\label{tab:human-edit}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Condition} & \textbf{3-class F1} & \textbf{Binary F1} & \textbf{$\Delta$ 3-class} & \textbf{$\Delta$ binary} \\
\midrule
Baseline          & 0.789 & 0.724 & ---       & ---       \\
Random 5\%        & 0.754 & 0.718 & $-3.5$\,pp & $-0.6$\,pp \\
Random 10\%       & 0.743 & 0.717 & $-4.6$\,pp & $-0.7$\,pp \\
Random 20\%       & 0.729 & 0.717 & $-6.0$\,pp & $-0.8$\,pp \\
LLM rephrase      & 0.755 & 0.662 & $-3.4$\,pp & $-6.3$\,pp \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The contrasting degradation patterns reveal that random noise and LLM rephrasing attack different aspects of the depth signal.
Random replacement degrades surface features (TTR, hapax ratio) that drive gen-0 separation, while preserving the reference-model entropy distribution that distinguishes gen-1 from gen-2+.
LLM rephrasing, by contrast, reshapes the entropy distribution itself, collapsing the depth-discriminative signal while leaving gen-0 separation relatively intact (the rephrased text is still recognizably machine-generated).
This suggests that depth fingerprinting is more vulnerable to systematic distributional manipulation than to surface-level noise---a practical consideration for deployment in settings where LLM-assisted editing is prevalent.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Shape stationarity: mechanistic hypothesis.}
Distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay) remain near-stationary across generation depths, while central-tendency features drift monotonically (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
We hypothesize that this reflects a decomposition of the autoregressive generation process: at each token position, the output distribution is determined jointly by model parameters (fixed) and conditioning context (varying).
Recursive generation progressively shifts context toward the model's high-probability regions---reducing entropy mean---but does not alter the softmax architecture or sampling hyperparameters that determine distributional shape.
This predicts that shape features should remain stationary until generation depth reaches the model's fixed-point distribution, a regime not yet observed in our chain lengths ($\leq$4 steps).
Sampling ablation is consistent with this account: depth signal is robust to moderate temperature variation (${\leq}0.3$\,pp for $t \in [0.5, 0.7]$) but degrades substantially at $t = 1.0$ ($-6$\,pp; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}), where the sampling mechanism itself becomes the dominant source of distributional shape variation, overwhelming the depth signal.

\paragraph{Prompt-type dependence.}
Differential depth response strength varies substantially across prompt types.
Continuation chains exhibit 16.9\% depth retention loss by gen-4, while elaboration chains retain 98.6\% of samples (Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}).
The 7-feature ensemble achieves within-type CV F1 of 0.781 for continuation vs.\ 0.730 for elaboration; cross-prompt-type transfer (LOPTO F1\,=\,0.753) confirms shared signal despite differing drift magnitudes.
These results bound depth fingerprinting's applicability: in near-paraphrastic settings (elaboration, rewriting), distributional drift attenuates more rapidly, consistent with semantic-preservation constraints acting as an anchor against distributional shift \cite{broken_telephone}.

\paragraph{Corpus-level vs.\ document-level utility.}
The practical value of depth estimation depends on the unit of analysis.
At the individual document level, gen-1 per-class F1\,=\,0.64 implies a 36\% misclassification rate---insufficient for automated filtering but suitable for flagging suspect documents for human review.
At the corpus level, aggregate depth composition can be estimated with substantially lower error: over $n$ documents, estimation error scales as $O(1/\sqrt{n})$, making corpus-level provenance characterization reliable even with moderate per-document accuracy.
The 3-class design explicitly targets the most informative boundaries: human vs.\ machine (gen-0 vs.\ gen-1+) and shallow vs.\ deep recursion (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+), where the distributional distinction is most actionable.

\paragraph{Relation to model collapse.}
Our results relate to, but are distinct from, model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse,self_consuming_mad}.
Model collapse describes distributional degradation when models are \emph{retrained} on their own outputs; we observe analogous drift---monotonic decrease in vocabulary diversity, compression of perplexity---in \emph{inference chains} without parameter updates.
Quantitatively, the magnitude differs: hapax ratio declines ${\sim}$14\% across 4 inference-chain depths, compared to catastrophic diversity loss reported after 5--10 retraining generations \cite{curse_of_recursion}.
We hypothesize that inference-chain drift represents an early, reversible stage of the same distributional narrowing process that becomes irreversible only when gradient updates amplify the shift.
This suggests depth fingerprinting features could serve as leading indicators: text exhibiting inference-chain drift signatures would, if recycled into training, accelerate the collapse regime.
Topic drift mediates rather than confounds this process: semantic narrowing accounts for less than 9\% of feature variance (maximum $R^2 = 0.082$ for entropy\_mean), and shape features are near-independent of semantic drift ($|\rho| = 0.068$).

\paragraph{Granularity ceiling.}
Five-class depth estimation yields LOGO F1\,$\approx$\,0.49 (vs.\ 0.762 for 3-class); gen-2 and gen-3 are inseparable (per-class F1\,$\approx$\,0.26), establishing three classes as the practical ceiling for handcrafted features (Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}).
QLoRA fine-tuning raises 3-class F1 to 0.905 (+11.6\,pp; Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}), confirming exploitable depth signal beyond summary statistics.

\paragraph{Robustness to post-generation editing.}
Depth features degrade gracefully under simulated editing: 20\% random token replacement reduces 3-class F1 by only 6.0\,pp, while LLM rephrasing drops binary F1 by 6.3\,pp (Appendix~\ref{app:human-edit}).
This asymmetry---surface noise is tolerable, systematic distributional manipulation is not---is consistent with depth signal residing in aggregate distributional properties rather than individual token choices.

\paragraph{Paraphrastic chains.}
Initial paraphrastic experiments exhibited reversed entropy--depth correlations ($\rho = +0.394$), but removing contaminated samples aligned correlations with continuation chains ($\rho = -0.533$), confirming the reversal was an artifact.
On clean data, paraphrastic chains achieve binary F1\,=\,0.671 (vs.\ 0.749 for continuation), consistent with faster convergence under semantic-preservation constraints \cite{broken_telephone}.
Cross-transfer is effective (para$\to$cont F1\,=\,0.770, cont$\to$para 0.743), indicating shared depth signal.

\paragraph{Instruct tuning.}
Instruction-tuned models show substantially weaker depth fingerprints (OLMo-Instruct LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 vs.\ 0.764 base; Qwen3-0.6B-Instruct 0.667 vs.\ 0.816 base under the 7-generator split; base-only yields 0.824, Table~\ref{tab:logo-results}).
Length-matched controls reduce correlations to near zero (all $|\rho| < 0.02$ for Qwen3-0.6B), and binary classification is near chance (F1\,$\approx$\,0.5), indicating that depth signal is not operationally detectable in instruct chains.
This justifies our restriction to base models: instruction tuning introduces distributional effects (output length regulation, format constraints) that dominate the subtler recursive drift signal, making base models the appropriate setting for isolating the generation mechanism.

\paragraph{Negative downstream finding.}
Depth-aware curation does not improve downstream language model quality over random subsampling (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).
This negative result carries positive information value: it rules out depth-based filtering as a data selection strategy, sparing practitioners from building depth-conditional pipelines that would not yield quality gains.
The dominant factor is data quantity, not depth composition---consistent with findings emphasizing data volume over curation sophistication \cite{self_consuming_mad}.
